fieldMarks: Prominent shoulder hump formed by the muscles of the forelegs.
Somewhat dished face profile and less prominent ears than a black bear.
Very long, straighter front claws suited to digging, not climbing.
Colour ranges from nearly white or blond to black; many have grizzled light fur on head and shoulders; colour alone does not separate brown from black bears.
Average adult male 250-350 kg; females about half that; coastal brown bears grow larger than interior grizzlies.
behavior: Generally solitary, but gathers at concentrated food such as salmon streams, sedge flats and carcasses.
Omnivorous: plants make up 80-90% of the diet (grasses, sedges, roots, berries), plus salmon, ground squirrels, carrion and newborn moose and caribou.
Home ranges usually 200-600 km2 for females and 900-1,800 km2 for males; in mountains, females and young keep to upper slopes while adult males use valley bottoms.
Dens in winter; cubs are born in the den in January-February and stay with the mother 2-3 years.
habitat: Coastal areas with spawning salmon and rich vegetation support the largest bears and highest densities; interior and northern 'grizzlies' range across tundra, mountains and forest.
range: Now limited to northwestern North America: Alaska, Yukon, Northwest Territories, Nunavut, British Columbia, Alberta, a few in Manitoba, and Montana, Wyoming and Idaho. Historically it ranged south into California and Mexico and east to about Manitoba.

lookalikes.name: American black bear
lookalikes.howToTell: Black bear lacks the prominent shoulder hump, has more prominent ears and shorter curved claws; colour is not reliable.

lookalikes.name: Polar bear
lookalikes.howToTell: Polar bear is more streamlined and lacks the shoulder hump.
